primary_cause: Collapsing rate expectations crushing NIM outlooks for banks. Fed emergency 50bps cut Mar 3. Rapid worsening of recession fears into Mar 12
secondary_factors: Rising expected credit losses. General financial-sector de-risking as markets questioned whether central-bank action would be enough
store_description: BAC's drop looks mostly like a rate-sensitive bank repricing. The Fed surprise cut signaled economic stress and by March 12 markets were in full panic after the Europe travel ban and policy disappointment which is exactly the mix that hits money-center banks through margin and credit channels.

primary_cause: Investors pricing sharp hit to billed business and travel-and-entertainment spend. Europe travel ban and fast deterioration in travel and entertainment activity directly relevant
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Credit-loss risk. Same lower-rate pressure hurting financials. Later company commentary confirmed volumes falling into March. No major AXP-specific release
store_description: AXP sold off harder than BAC because its revenue mix was more exposed to discretionary and cross-border spend just as governments imposed travel restrictions and markets started discounting a sudden stop in consumer and corporate travel.

primary_cause: Semiconductor-wide COVID demand and supply fears plus pre-earnings risk-off selling. Broadcom reported after close Mar 12 — $5.9B Q1 revenue $2.2B FCF $6.4B cash — not bad
secondary_factors: Broad tech multiple compression. Uncertainty around enterprise and hardware spending. Same-day decline not driven by bad pre-drop earnings miss
store_description: Because AVGO's earnings landed after the bell and were not obviously weak on headline numbers the March 12 drop is best explained by a severe semiconductor derating during the COVID crash rather than a discrete Broadcom negative.

primary_cause: No major Amazon-specific negative. Broad market panic and repricing of consumer and enterprise demand risk despite Amazon's later pandemic upside
secondary_factors: Logistics uncertainty. Labor and disruption risk. Sell-first mentality across megacap tech. Not yet rewarding Amazon for e-commerce demand pull-forward
store_description: On March 12 investors were not yet rewarding Amazon for e-commerce demand pull-forward. They were treating it as a large-cap cyclical and tech exposure in a crash driven by policy panic and shutdown risk. The stock's decline was meaningful but smaller than many cyclicals.

primary_cause: No clear AMT-specific negative. Indiscriminate REIT and equity deleveraging during COVID liquidation wave
secondary_factors: Concern that tenants emerging-market currencies and financing conditions could all worsen if pandemic spread
store_description: AMT fell less than many cyclicals which is consistent with its relatively defensive tower model but it still got hit as investors sold liquid REITs and anything balance-sheet-sensitive into the March 12 funding panic.

primary_cause: No major Amgen-specific negative. Broad biotech and pharma de-risking within violent market selloff
secondary_factors: Concern about clinical-trial disruption physician-visit slowdowns and general liquidity-driven selling
store_description: AMGN's decline was larger than expected for a pure defensive move but in the March 12 liquidation even high-quality healthcare names were sold for cash. No stock-specific news catalyst in the 3-day window more convincing than the marketwide COVID panic.

primary_cause: Severe semiconductor equipment selloff on fears of fab and customer spending delays. No AMAT-specific pre-drop announcement
secondary_factors: China exposure. Export and supply logistics worries. Broad tech de-risking. Highly cyclical capex name into fast-moving global shutdown
store_description: AMAT's outsized decline versus the market fits the view that investors were repricing a highly cyclical capex name into a fast-moving global shutdown not reacting to a single company headline. The stock behaved like a high-beta semiconductor-equipment proxy for collapsing visibility.

primary_cause: Broad software multiple compression and enterprise-spending fear into the crash. Adobe reported after close Mar 12 — record Q1 revenue $3.09B 19% YoY growth $0.07/share hit from event cancellations
secondary_factors: Cancellation of live events. Uncertainty around business-software demand if customers froze budgets. Daytime selloff not caused by weak reported quarter
store_description: Since the earnings release came after the market closed and the headline numbers were strong ADBE's intraday drop reads as macro and software derating rather than earnings disappointment. Investors were dumping even premium-growth software because valuation mattered less than liquidity on March 12.

primary_cause: Investors anticipating weaker consulting demand as clients froze discretionary projects. Did not cut guidance until Mar 19
secondary_factors: General market panic. Fear of delayed enterprise digital and transformation spending. Preemptive rather than headline-driven. No Accenture-specific negative release
store_description: ACN sold off as a high-quality services name whose revenue depends on corporate confidence and that confidence was evaporating rapidly by March 12. The later March 19 revenue-forecast cut validated that investors were right to worry.

primary_cause: Broad-market healthcare selling partially offset by possibility Abbott could benefit from diagnostics demand. Not yet received later March FDA emergency authorization
secondary_factors: Uncertainty about timing of test approvals and disruption to non-COVID medical activity. Fell much less than high-beta cyclicals
store_description: ABT fell much less than the market's high-beta cyclicals which makes sense because diagnostics was a relative safe haven but it still got dragged down in the March 12 liquidation. No obvious negative Abbott-specific headline in the prior 3 days.

primary_cause: No material AbbVie-specific negative. Broad pharma and biotech de-risking during market break
secondary_factors: Concern around still-pending Allergan integration and COVID disruption to physician-administered and aesthetics-linked demand
store_description: ABBV traded more like a risk asset than a pure defensive on March 12 likely because investors were reducing exposure to leveraged M&A stories and any pharma name with non-core elective exposure. No better stock-specific catalyst in that exact window.

primary_cause: Renewed fear that Apple faced both supply disruption and global demand shock. Already warned Feb 17 COVID hurting supply and sales. Mar 14 announced stores outside Greater China would close temporarily
secondary_factors: Retail-store disruption. Weaker device demand. Megacap-tech liquidation. Week of Mar 9 moved most staff to work from home
store_description: AAPL's March 12 drop was not about a fresh one-day miss but about investors realizing the problem had moved from China supply to global retail and demand. The later store-closure announcement came just after the drop and reinforced what the market was already starting to price.

primary_cause: Fear that elective surgery volumes and da Vinci procedure growth would drop sharply. Hospitals began preparing to postpone elective procedures
secondary_factors: Capital-equipment spending risk at hospitals. General medtech de-risking. Reuters documented widespread elective-surgery postponements days later
store_description: ISRG is especially exposed to procedure deferrals so even before formal pause announcements became widespread the market had a clear reason to sell it as the pandemic escalated. Later confirmation that hospitals were suspending elective procedures fits ISRG's sharp March 12 move.

primary_cause: Repricing of NBCUniversal and consumer-media exposure as COVID restrictions spread. Theme-park film and advertising exposure highly vulnerable to shutdowns
secondary_factors: Ad-market weakness. General market stress partly offset by defensive cable broadband business. No single Comcast headline dominated
store_description: Comcast's drop was larger than a pure utility-style business would suggest because investors were focusing on NBCUniversal's cyclical segments not just cable connectivity. The 2020 results later showed COVID had materially negative effects on NBCUniversal and Sky.

primary_cause: Investors pricing higher credit-card and consumer loan losses. Fast-rising recession and consumer-credit concerns
secondary_factors: Lower rates. Funding fears. Broad financial-sector liquidation. Business mix more directly tied to unsecured consumer credit. No major COF-specific announcement
store_description: COF fell more than money-center banks because its business mix was more directly tied to unsecured consumer credit just as the market started bracing for a jump in charge-offs and unemployment. One of the clearest credit-cycle proxy casualties of March 12.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Boeing planned to draw down remainder of $13.8B loan on Mar 11. Airlines slashing capacity and raising liquidity. Still stuck in 737 MAX crisis
secondary_factors: Unresolved MAX grounding. Broad market panic. Combination of airline-demand shock and Boeing-specific liquidity and stress concerns
store_description: BA was not just a macro victim. A nearly one-fifth drop makes sense because March 12 hit Boeing at the intersection of three problems: airlines suddenly had no demand customers were preserving cash and Boeing itself was taking defensive financing steps while still dealing with the MAX overhang.

primary_cause: Broad market liquidation not deteriorating near-term sales. Visible pantry-loading demand. No major negative Costco-specific release
secondary_factors: Concern that panic-buying would come with margin pressure labor and sanitation costs and product-mix distortions. Relatively smaller drop versus market
store_description: COST's relatively smaller drop versus the market fits a name with strong traffic but still exposed to the general sell everything phase of the crash. This looks much more like indiscriminate de-risking than a Costco-specific bad-news event.

primary_cause: Semiconductor repricing on COVID supply-chain and end-demand fears. Tech sector dealing with visible supply-chain disruption and uncertainty around hardware and component demand
secondary_factors: Data-center and PC demand uncertainty. China manufacturing risk. Broad Nasdaq weakness
store_description: INTC's drop fits the same pattern as AMAT and AVGO: investors were selling semis as highly liquid cyclical tech with poor short-term visibility. No discrete Intel-specific 3-day headline that explains the move better than the sectorwide COVID reset.

primary_cause: Oil-price collapse. Reuters Mar 9 oil plunged ~25% after Saudi-Russia price war. Recession fears possible capex cuts
secondary_factors: Investor concern over shale and equity cash flows if crude stayed low. Both exogenous commodity crash and pandemic-driven demand collapse
store_description: COP was one of the easier names to attribute: the stock was getting hit by both an exogenous commodity crash and a pandemic-driven demand collapse at the same time. The causal chain was unusually direct through realized commodity prices and cash-flow expectations.

primary_cause: Investors repricing Honeywell aerospace business for severe aviation downturn. Airlines cutting capex and scrambling for liquidity. Honeywell reaffirmed 2020 outlook Mar 10 but reassurance did not hold
secondary_factors: Industrial cyclicality. Supply-chain disruption. Mar 10 reaffirmation quickly looked stale in rapidly worsening environment
store_description: HON's double-digit decline suggests the market stopped believing near-term industrial guidance almost immediately. With airline customers slashing spending and Boeing under pressure Honeywell's aerospace exposure likely became the dominant stock-specific driver on top of the broader crash.
